title: Epitaxial growth of WO3 on r-plane sapphire by hot-filament metal-oxide deposition using CO2 as a precursor
authors: Laurent Souqui, Lewis J. Adams, Andreas Tsampanakis, David Rehnlund Maibach, Per Eklund
abstract: The deposition of epitaxial films of WO3 by hot-filament metal-oxide deposition using CO2 as a precursor was demonstrated. The films were obtained at a low growth rate of 0.25 nm/min. The optical properties of the film were assessed by variable-angle spectroscopic ellipsometry, indicating transparency across the visible spectrum and high absorption above 3 eV.
summary: This paper reports the successful epitaxial growth of WO3 thin films on r-plane sapphire using a hot-filament CVD method with CO2 as the precursor. Characterization confirmed the film's crystalline quality, epitaxial orientation, and optical properties, showing transparency in the visible range and a band gap consistent with stoichiometric WO3.
main_problem: The study aimed to demonstrate the epitaxial growth of WO3 thin films on r-plane sapphire using a hot-filament metal-oxide deposition (HFMOD) technique with CO2 as the precursor.
main_result: Epitaxial WO3 films were successfully grown with a low growth rate, exhibiting optical transparency in the visible spectrum and confirming crystal structures consistent with orthorhombic or monoclinic phases.
method: The films were deposited using hot-filament CVD, and characterization involved X-ray Diffraction (XRD) for structural analysis and Variable-angle Spectroscopic Ellipsometry (VASE) for optical property measurement.
model_or_system: The physical system is the deposition of WO3 thin films onto r-plane sapphire (alpha-Al2O3) using a hot-filament reactor. The growth process is controlled by the reaction of tungsten wires with CO2 at elevated temperatures.
key_observables: Optical constants (epsilon_1, epsilon_2), absorption coefficient, epitaxial relationships (e.g., WO3(001)//alpha-Al2O3(0112C2)), and crystal phase identification (monoclinic/orthorhombic).
important_parameters: Low growth rate of 0.25 nm/min; substrate temperature of 450°C; measurement range up to 5.9 eV.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that CO2 acts as the necessary oxidizing species for the deposition reaction, confirmed by comparison with Ar deposition.
figures_summary: Figures show XRD scans comparing CO2 vs. Ar deposition, GID patterns confirming epitaxial relationships, pole figures detailing crystal orientation, and VASE plots showing the energy dependence of the dielectric function components.
paper_structure: The paper follows a structure of demonstrating the deposition process, characterizing the crystal structure using XRD (including epitaxial relationships), and characterizing the optical properties using VASE to confirm material stoichiometry and band gap.
why_interesting: While primarily materials science, the precise control over thin film growth, crystallinity, and optical band structure using controlled chemical precursors (CO2) is relevant to developing quantum optical components or substrates for quantum devices.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: (a) Extended 2θ/ω scans of films deposited on sapphire with CO2 for 30 min, 120 min, and without CO2 (Ar). (b) Close- up around the tungsten oxide 002 peak

Figure 1(a) shows 2q/w scans from films deposited with CO2 for 30 min and 120 min, and for comparison films deposited with pure Ar. The XRD scan from the film deposited with CO2 for 30 min exhibits distinct Laue fringes (Figure 1(b)), meaning that films of high crystalline quality are obtained. The fringes for the films deposited for 120 min are difficult to resolve because of their higher thickness of 30 nm, as measured by ellipsometry, corresponding to an average growth rate of 0.25 nm/min.

Fig. 2: GID patterns of the 120 min-deposited sample taken along the [110] direction of sapphire, and rotated by φ = 45°, 90° and 135° and Ψ = 89.5°. Low intensity, non-indexed peaks and shoulders match with Kβ radiation.
Fig. 3: Pole figures recorded at 2θ = 35.68°. The three set of circles correspond three groups of poles.

Fig. 4: Optical properties of a 30-nm WO3 thin film deposited on r-cut sapphire a) real part of the dielectric function, b) imaginary part of the dielectric function, and c) absorption coefficient. The feature at 4.5 eV is a fitting artifact.
